writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Attorney General, what assessment she has made of the potential impact of the time taken for digital evidence analysis on the time taken for the Crown Prosecution Service to make charging decisions in rape cases.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Delivering timely justice for victims of rape and serious sexual assault is a priority for this government. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) is working closely with the police and other criminal justice partners to ensure that access to justice.

The increase in scale and scope of digital technologies is creating new avenues for abuse and exploitation. As a result, the volume of digital evidence that is required for a case to be investigated and a charging decision to be made has increased significantly, placing increased pressure on criminal justice agencies.

A key component of the CPS’ National Operating Model (NOM), launched in July 2023, is strengthened collaboration with policing services and an emphasis on improved early interactions at the start of a case. This includes an offer of early advice, enabling the police to seek advice from a CPS prosecutor at a much earlier point in the case, and a meeting at pre-charge stage. These early discussion between police and prosecutors can help identify which electronic devices, accounts, time periods, and types of data are relevant to the case reducing the amount of time taken to review digital evidence.

Since the launch of the CPS’ NOM, the median number of days between a case being referred and a decision to charge fell from 31 days in 2022/23, to 6 days in 2025/26. This indicates that, despite the increased demands regarding digital evidence, the CPS’ efforts to improve collaboration with policing has resulted in overall improvements in timeliness in adult rape-flagged cases.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, with reference to the Government's policy of using public procurement to back British businesses, what definition the Government uses of a British business for procurement purposes; and whether that definition takes account of (a) ownership, (b) intellectual property rights, (c) operational control and (d) supply-chain dependencies.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The current definition is easily met by suppliers without genuine presence in the UK, which masks the UK's actual reliance on foreign supply chains through data captured on the central digital platform.

The Government announced at Budget that it will publish a new definition of a “UK Supplier” by January 2027. This will be based on genuine UK economic presence and will provide better procurement data, improving supply chain transparency and allowing us to bolster our resilience. The exact criteria are still being developed.

This reform, among others, will be introduced into legislation when Parliamentary time allows. The definition and future reforms will balance our domestic interests while complying with our trade agreements as our supply chains are highly integrated and maintaining our trade partnerships benefits both the UK and our closest allies to achieve our economic and security objectives.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, how long on average claimants of Civil Service Survivor Benefit have waited from bereavement to first payment in each of the last five years.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Cabinet Office awarded Capita the contract to administer the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) in November 2023 under the previous government. The current delays facing scheme members and bereaved families are entirely unacceptable, and the Government continues to hold Capita to account for delivery of the service, applying all contractual levers. This includes withholding £9.9 million in contract payments for undelivered milestones. We intend to seek to recover all the Government’s delay-related costs, and that Capita bear the costs of their failure, not the taxpayer.

In relation to the specific statistical information requested on average waiting times from bereavement to first survivor benefit payment over the last five years (PQ 43870) and the number of open survivor benefit claims initiated prior to January 2026 (PQ 43878), the specific level of detail requested is not readily available. There is currently no standard report linking both the date of bereavement and the date of first survivor benefit payment, and providing reliable figures would require a manual case-by-case review. Similarly, while open bereavement cases predating January 2026 can be identified, determining whether a survivor benefit is payable has not yet been completed across all open cases, meaning establishing an accurate figure would also require a manual review.

Ministers have been clear that the issues and delays facing civil servants and pension scheme members and bereaved families are unacceptable. We continue to hold Capita to account for delivery, and Ministers and officials have met repeatedly with senior Capita executives to do so, including emphasising the impact on the civil servants and their dependents who have experienced unacceptably poor service and poor communication. To provide assurance on Capita’s approach, an independent Remedial Adviser (Grant Thornton) was appointed at Capita’s expense to test and validate their operational recovery plans. Following receipt of the Remedial Adviser's report, a substantive update was provided to Parliament on 26 October.

The independent report concluded that Capita’s initial rectification plans and technology execution were wholly insufficient. While Capita reported meeting self-imposed targets in September for workable stock, this did not constitute full-service recovery or reflect members' lived experiences. Consequently, the Government has taken definitive action and agreed a new Recovery Plan with Capita.

This new plan comprises five workstreams focused on case complexity, key projects, and technology infrastructure. In administering survivor benefits, Capita communicates directly with the survivor rather than liaising with individual government departments; however, Capita's wider operational performance is closely monitored and challenged through multiple structured lines of open communication across government departments, including cross-departmental working between the Cabinet Office and HMRC. Cabinet Office officials now have access to Capita’s systems and data, so that we can be assured as to the completeness of information reported, and expert teams have been deployed to work with Capita both in designing their plan and to assure their delivery. To ensure old cases do not remain in backlogs, Capita has committed to writing to every member with a complex case within the next month and to provide access to a dedicated specialist contact line. Furthermore, to guarantee transparency, data-focussed fortnightly scheme performance updates will now be published on the pension scheme website which cover the whole caseload, rather than specific subsets.

Further commercial, legal, and operational options remain on the table, and work is continuing on actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring this pension scheme back in-house.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, with reference to Civil Service Pensions Taskforce update 16, published on 3 September 2026, how many of the approximately 900 retirement quotations remaining from the backlog at the end of August related to deferred members; and how many of those members had been waiting for a quotation for more than (a) six months and (b) 12 months.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Cabinet Office awarded Capita the contract to administer the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) in November 2023 under the previous government. The current delays facing scheme members are entirely unacceptable, and the Government continues to hold Capita firmly to account for delivery of the service, applying all available contractual levers. This includes withholding £9.9 million in contract payments for undelivered milestones, and we intend to seek to recover all the Government’s delay-related costs so that Capita bears the costs of its failure, not the taxpayer.

As noted in subsequent Taskforce updates and Ministerial statements, the c.900 figure reported on 3 September reflected Capita's narrow legacy MI subset, for which a further breakdown is not readily available, rather than the full gross operational caseload across all workstreams. Following the independent Remedial Adviser's review, reporting was reset on 5 October 2026 to capture the whole-system view across Workstream 1 (Complex), Workstream 2 (Core BAU), and Workstream 3 (BAU Non-KPI), and Cabinet Office officials now have access to Capita data to provide additional assurance and analysis.

In relation to requests for CSPS retirement quotations recorded as closed without a quotation having been issued since 1 December 2025 (PQ 44025), the level of detail requested is not available. As quotation issuance is not currently captured as a standalone reportable field in Capita’s management information, and historical bulk closures were not differentiated on that basis, establishing an accurate figure would require a manual case-by-case review, which could only be undertaken at disproportionate cost. To strengthen operational controls, reporting integrity, and quality assurance across all casework, the Government has agreed a new five-workstream Recovery Plan with Capita following the independent Remedial Adviser’s (Grant Thornton) review. Cabinet Office officials now have direct access to Capita’s systems and data to verify the completeness and accuracy of reporting, alongside an independent technical review by the Government Internal Audit Agency (GIAA) and deployed Civil Service expert teams assuring operational processes and delivery.

The eligibility for a hardship loan is restricted to active scheme members who have either retired or partially retired directly from a Civil Service employer since 1 January 2025 and face payment delays. Because these bridging funds are legally classified as employee-employer loans, they cannot be extended to deferred members, surviving spouses, or dependants due to the lack of an active employment link. Deferred groups and vulnerable dependants are instead directed to Capita for urgent internal prioritisation via Cabinet Office -monitored workflows. We are working tightly with internal teams to ensure that those who cannot access a loan have their core files fast-tracked through the system via our triage managers.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, what recent steps her Department has taken to ensure key national infrastructure is protected from future cyberattacks.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is working to improve resilience to cyber risks across the UK economy and drive organisations to take effective action. We are scaling up our work to make the internet automatically safer, building in basic protections to benefit all UK businesses, organisations and citizens.

This work includes ongoing engagement and support to owners and operators of Critical National Infrastructure (CNI) in the UK to maintain and improve the cyber resilience of our most critical systems and assets.

This week I chaired a closed-door threat briefing in Whitehall with CEOs from CNI providers. This builds on ongoing work to strengthen the UK’s resilience against hostile activity by providing tailored security advice for businesses. This, and the one chaired by the Minister for the Armed Forces with the Defence Industry, draw on the UK’s world-class intelligence capabilities and a commitment to a whole of society approach to security and resilience.

The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, introduced on 12 November 2025, will strengthen the UK’s cyber defences and ensure that the essential and digital services that the public relies upon are more secure in the face of cyber criminals and state actors who want to disrupt our way of life.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what steps her Department is taking to support long established local newspapers, particularly those serving smaller communities.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is concerned about the long-term financial sustainability of local newspapers and local journalism and recognises the vital role they play in scrutinising local institutions and reflecting communities’ views and perspectives. We are committed to ensuring a healthy and plural local media for the benefit of communities and citizens across the UK and published Amplify: The Local Media Action Plan earlier this year.

The actions we are taking will support local media organisations across the country to innovate and adapt their business models for the online world, while incentivising and encouraging the production of high quality, trustworthy news on which smaller communities depend. As part of the Action Plan, we launched a Local News Fund worth £6m in 2026/27 and up to a further £6m in 2027/28, to help ensure the long term provision of local news, which funded 50 local media organisations. Local media faces a complex range of challenges and funding represents just one aspect of our approach. It will help the industry adapt in the short-medium term, before longer term measures set out in the Plan begin to take effect in helping enable a free, plural and thriving online local media ecosystem. A list of successful grantees for 2026/27 can be found here.

As part of the Action Plan, we have also

  • Launched an Inspiring the Future journalism careers campaign in the North West to inspire young people to pursue careers in local media. The campaign will conclude shortly and, subject to funding and evaluation, we hope to roll it out nationwide.

  • Uplifted the Community Radio Fund, now worth £1m over each of the next 3 years. The Fund closed for bids for funding in this financial year on 14 October.

  • Published our Media Green Paper, which sought views on a range of matters including options to require social media to make news content from commercial local (and national) news publishers as well as public service media, prominent and easily discoverable.

We are also planning to launch a public consultation on statutory notices by the end of this year, we will be responding in due course to our BBC Charter Green Paper including in relation to the role of the BBC in the local news market, and we will shortly publish a refreshed National Action Plan for the Safety of Journalists.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what recent steps her Department has taken to strengthen protections for the families of people impacted by press intrusion.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
We recognise that for victims and their families, unacceptable incidents of harassment and intrusion from the media cause significant distress, and the Secretary of State has met affected individuals and families.

The UK has a self-regulatory system for the press, which is independent from the government. An independent press is important for press freedom and to ensure the public has access to accurate and trustworthy information from a range of different sources. However, we expect all publishers to operate within the bounds of the law and adhere to high ethical and professional standards, as well as ensure appropriate routes to redress if these standards are not met.

The Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO) and the Independent Monitor of the Press (Impress) were established following the findings of the Leveson Report in 2012, to ensure these high standards are met. Their codes provide guidelines on a range of areas, including on accuracy, bereavement, privacy and harassment. If these regulators find that a newspaper has broken the code of conduct, they can order corrections. IPSO can also order critical adjudications and Impress can levy fines.

The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) is working with partners including the National Police Chiefs’ Council and other government departments to improve the identification and enforcement of number plate crime.

The Government is reviewing the existing arrangements for the supply of number plates to enable tighter checks on suppliers and the plates they supply. Options being considered include reviewing fees, the structure of the scheme, resources and funding.

I have written to the largest online marketplaces to ask them to work with officials to help tackle the illegal supply of number plates.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, , whether his Department has evaluated Capita's readiness and competence to deliver the Synergy contract within the agreed timescale and budget, and to satisfy the contract's Key Performance Indicators.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Capita's appointment followed a robust two-year procurement process supported by commercial, legal and programme delivery experts, with functional experts from all four departments evaluating final bids. The procurement met all regulatory requirements, passed HM Treasury and Cabinet Office controls, and assessed bids on a 70% quality and 30% cost basis, reflecting the critical nature of the services involved

The programme has evaluated, and continues to monitor, Capita's ability to deliver its obligations under the Synergy contract. Capita is currently performing against its contractual obligations.

Delivery will be subject to continuing commercial and programme assurance, with the contract containing a range of performance management mechanisms, including service credits, delay payments, milestone retention, rectification plans, step-in rights and termination provisions, which are supported by experienced commercial and contract management professionals who monitor delivery against contractual commitments and service performance measures, including KPI’s.

Before any services transition, technical, payroll, business and operational testing will demonstrate that the service is ready, and the programme retains control of the final go-live decision. In addition, contractual arrangements with the current supplier mean there is no cliff edge requiring Synergy to transition before services are fully assured.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, what assessment his Department has made of the accessibility of online job application platforms for neurodivergent applicants who use (a) screen readers and (b) other assistive technology.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Employers have a responsibility under the Equality Act 2010 to make appropriate reasonable adjustments for disabled job applicants, including to recruitment processes. Additionally, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 provide an internationally recognised standard for web content accessibility, including for people who use assistive technologies.

The Government is also aware that recruitment processes can present barriers for neurodivergent people. The independent Expert Academic Panel on Neurodiversity’s report, published in October, sets out recommendations to improve recruitment, retention and progression. We will continue working with employers and stakeholders to understand how we can better support inclusive recruitment practices.

The Government recognises that technology is rapidly transforming how people live and work and that assistive and accessible technology can enable independence, greater inclusion and participation for people who can face barriers getting into work and at work due to health and disability. The Secretary of State for Work and Pensions has brought together representatives from across the technology industry, and Disabled People’s Organisations, to identify how we can remove the barriers preventing users of assistive technology from finding and keeping work.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, what steps he is taking to ensure delivery platforms are responsible for the safety of their riders who use e-bikes or e-scooters.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government expects delivery platforms to take appropriate steps to support the safety of riders using their services, including e-bikes and e-scooters. Health and safety protections apply to all workers, including those in the gig economy, and the government works with regulators to promote safe riding and driving for work.

All workers, including gig workers, have the right to work in environments where risks to their health and safety are properly controlled. Companies should provide gig workers with information and instruction appropriate to the risks they face, equivalent to that provided to employees. However, a key consideration is that gig economy riders are predominantly self-employed and it remains the responsibility of the gig worker/rider to follow that information and instruction. Where a business offers gig workers/riders training for example on vehicle maintenance or driving standards, participation is ultimately a matter for the rider.

HSE provide guidance for gig economy, agency and temporary workers. Riders also have duties under health and safety legislation to ensure that their undertaking does not expose others to risks. In practical terms, this means that riders are responsible for the work equipment they provide themselves, including their personal bicycles.

HSE have also worked with the Department for Transport to produce guidance on driving and riding safely for work. This guidance sets out the responsibilities of riders and gig workers for their own safety and that of others.

writtenQuestions.answerText:

Health and safety legislation applies to self-employed riders, who have duties under Section 3 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 to conduct their work in a way that does not put others at risk. Where riders provide their own vehicles for work, they are responsible for ensuring those vehicles are safe and legally compliant.

Companies should provide gig workers with information and instruction appropriate to the risks they face, and all workers, including gig workers, have the right to work in environments where risks to their health and safety are properly controlled. However, it remains the responsibility of the gig worker/rider to follow that information and instruction.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the number of NHS mental health trusts that automatically share free-text clinical progress notes, including psychotherapy notes, through shared care records.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
I refer the Noble Lord to the answer provided in the House of Commons on 23 November in response to Question 35420, which, for ease of reference, is reproduced below:

In respect of the Single Patient Record, discussions are ongoing on a range of practical issues about its scope and operation, and that includes determining what arrangements should apply to the sharing of psychotherapy and psychological therapy records, including the highly personal and private information contained in the notes of therapy sessions.

No final decisions have been made in this area, and we are extremely mindful of the views of patient groups, therapy professionals and other stakeholders, and of the debates that have previously taken place in other contexts about the need to prevent inappropriate third party access to confidential therapy notes. We will provide further updates in due course.

More generally, the controllers of a shared care record are required under the common law duty of confidentiality to communicate adequately to their local communities the existence and purposes of a shared care record, its impact on individuals and their right to object to some or all of their confidential patient information being included within that shared record.

Furthermore, the controllers of the shared care record must also ensure that they comply with UK General Data Protection Regulation requirements that data is processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, making reasonable efforts to ensure that individuals are informed about how their personal data is used.

In accordance with s251B of the Health and Social Care Act 2012, it is appropriate for clinicians to share information through a shared care record with other clinicians responsible for a patient’s care, unless that patient objects, or it is reasonable for them to believe that the patient would object. When it is necessary for direct care purposes, for example in an emergency situation, and those purposes are consistent with the reasonable expectations of the individual patient, health professionals will also rely on an assumption of consent to share essential information with other professionals responsible for the patient’s care.

However, as with all health records, there are strict rules and guidance in place to prevent unauthorised, inappropriate and unjustifiable access to confidential patient information by NHS employees, regardless of whether that information is held on a shared record, with staff who breach those rules facing suspension, dismissal and potential prosecution.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government how they intend to ensure that (1) the burdens on suppliers of medical devices subject to the current review of Part IX of the Drug Tariff are fully assessed and mitigated for further waves of the review, and (2) Wave 2 of the review is not launched until any revisions to the enhanced assessment framework are discussed and agreed with the Drug Tariff committee before being published on the NHS Business Services Authority website.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The initial impact assessment for the changes to Part IX of the Drug Tariff considered the burdens on suppliers, and following completion of Wave 1, the assumptions made in the impact assessment will be revisited to see if they proved accurate. The application process will also be reviewed to identify opportunities for improvement.

The evaluation of Wave 1 will include surveys of industry, feedback from clinical and patient representatives involved in the Wave 1 expert panels, and consultation with the Drug Tariff Committee. Wave 2 will not be launched until any changes are made to the assessment framework or application process in light of the lessons learnt from Wave 1.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government, further to the Written Answer by Baroness Merron on 20 July (HL1592), how many tests were performed at each individual community diagnostics centre in each month of 2026; and how many tests were provided in total in 2025.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
No complete assessment of the number of tests performed at each individual community diagnostics centre (CDC) in each month of 2026 has been made, but I can confirm that 8.33 million tests were performed CDCs in 2025. The Department does not centrally hold data on the number of staff working in each individual CDC.

On budgets for CDCs, I refer the Noble Lord to the answer provided on 15 April 2025 in response to Question HL6412 which, for ease of reference, is reproduced below:

The information requested is not held centrally in the format requested, and could only be obtained at disproportionate cost.

NHS England publishes a monthly report on diagnostic activity for the 15 modalities that make up the Diagnostics Waiting Times and Activity collection. This includes details of activity undertaken in CDCs for those 15 modalities. This is published on the NHS.UK website, in an online only format. It is not, however, a complete record of all CDC activity.

NHS England also publishes a quarterly dataset of all CDC activity at a national level. This is also published on the NHS.UK website, in an online only format. The latest published CDC management information details that CDCs have delivered over 13.9 million additional tests since July 2021.

NHS England’s CDC programme has been supported by a capital budget of £1.48 billion across 2022/23 to 2024/25.

The Elective Reform Plan, published in January 2025, committed to expanding existing CDCs, as well as building up to five new ones in 2025/26, to support the National Health Service to return to meeting the elective waiting time constitutional standard. The plan also commits to CDCs opening 12 hours per day, seven days a week, and delivering more same-day tests and consultations, with an expanded range of tests.

The 2025/25 capital guidance confirmed that £1.65 billion of capital funding will be allocated to support NHS performance across secondary and emergency care, across 2025/26 more broadly. This includes £450 million which has been provisionally allocated for diagnostics, which includes CDCs, partly to expand existing and build new CDCs. £20 million has also been allocated directly to relevant trusts via a separate processes for CDC pathway productivity.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government who holds the encryption keys for identifiable patient data in the NHS Federated Data Platform; and whether staff of Palantir Technologies UK Ltd or its sub-contractors can decrypt that data without NHS England releasing an encryption key for a specified task.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
NHS England owns the encryption keys used to protect data within the NHS Federated Data Platform. The keys are generated and managed by the Privacy Enhancing Technology (PET) software and are held securely within the Amazon Web Services’ infrastructure supporting PET. Staff of Palantir Technologies UK Ltd or its subcontractors cannot independently access an encryption key to decrypt or re-identify patient data.

Where re-identification is required, it must first be specifically approved by NHS England through the relevant Data Set Approval process, including the treatment specification, intended recipient, and appropriate encryption/domain key name.

There have been five non-National Health Service enrolment administration role requests approved for access to data in the National Data Integration Tenant (NDIT). All were employed by Palantir UK, with a maximum of three roles in place at any time. There are currently three active enrolment administration roles employed by Palantir UK. All have Security Clearance in place in line with NHS England vetting policy and are subject to NDIT Governance and Audit processes.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what consideration they have given to the creation of a National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline for Tourette syndrome which would establish nationally recognised standards for diagnosis and management of the condition.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises the need to improve consistency in the diagnosis and management of Tourette syndrome. Integrated care boards are responsible for commissioning appropriate diagnostic and treatment pathways according to local need, while NHS England’s Getting It Right First Time programme uses data to identify and address unwarranted variation, working with local systems to support clearer and more consistent diagnostic and treatment pathways. This work also includes the appointment of a clinical lead for children and young people's neurodevelopmental services focused on improving assessment and management.

The National Institute for Care Excellence (NICE) decided in March 2025 not to prioritise developing a dedicated guideline on Tourette syndrome because the topic overlaps heavily with other conditions and many existing challenges relate to service provision, where NICE guidance would have limited impact. However, existing NICE guidance on suspected neurological conditions includes recommendations on tics and involuntary movements, and NICE has confirmed that a clinical knowledge summary on the topic of tics and Tourette syndrome is due to be published on its website in February 2027.

To improve professional awareness, NHS England’s Learning Hub provides an e-learning module titled Understanding Tourette Syndrome, developed in partnership with Tourette’s Action. In addition to the general module, which was added in August 2023, the Learning Hub also hosts a dedicated companion module, Understanding Tourette syndrome for GPs and Health Professionals, which was added in October 2024 and updated in January 2026.

We recognise the importance of appropriate data to support service planning and will continue to work with NHS England to improve care and reduce unwarranted variation for people with Tourette syndrome.

writtenQuestions.answerText:
In April 2026, the child sexual exploitation and abuse (CSEA) reporting duty came into force for user-to-user services under the Online Safety Act 2023 (OSA). The duty requires in-scope providers to report detected and unreported CSEA content to the National Crime Agency (NCA).

The CSEA reporting duty increases law enforcement’s ability to safeguard children, identify offenders, and prevent re-victimisation. Since the reporting duty came into force, in-scope user-to-user services have been registering with the NCA and submitting reports in accordance with the Reporting Regulations, which sets out the information that must be included in reports submitted to the NCA.

The Government continues to work closely with the NCA to support delivery of the requirement. The CSEA reporting duty, associated regulations and operational processes are kept under review to ensure they remain relevant, appropriate and proportionate.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what plans they have, if any, to permit taxi and private hire vehicle operators to rely on right to work checks undertaken by local licensing authorities when issuing or renewing driver licences as a statutory excuse against civil penalties.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
From 1 October 2026, the Government’s changes to the Right to Work Scheme extended the requirements to conduct right to work checks to organisations that engage individuals to provide work or services under their company name. This included operators in the taxi and private hire vehicle sector.

While local authority licensing checks form an important part of the existing system, reliance on these checks alone would create ambiguity as to where accountability rests if illegal working is identified, particularly where services are provided through platform-based models. Under the legislation the legal responsibility to conduct checks sits with the organisation engaging the individual to provide work or services. It is by carrying out the prescribed right to work check that employers or operators can establish a statutory excuse against liability for a civil penalty.

writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is determined to prevent dangerous substances from reaching our communities including through the online sale of illegal drugs. This includes considering how technologies such as artificial intelligence can strengthen detection and disruption efforts.

Across law enforcement, work is underway to develop and harness these capabilities. The Government has launched PoliceAI, a new national centre dedicated to the responsible development, testing and scaling of AI across all forces in England and Wales.

The Online Safety Act 2023 places clear legal duties on online platforms to implement systems and processes that prevent users from encountering illegal content, including that which facilitates the sale of illegal drugs, and to ensure that such content is swiftly removed once they become aware of it.

Ofcom, as the Act’s independent regulator, has our full backing to take action against non-compliant services, including issuing fines of up to £18 million or 10% of a company’s qualifying worldwide annual revenue (whichever is greater). In the most serious cases, Ofcom can seek a court order to block a site in the UK.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what progress his Department has made on developing a Defence-wide doctrine for uncrewed warfare.
writtenQuestions.answerText:

The Department's approach is to integrate uncrewed capabilities across the full spectrum of military operations where they offer an operational advantage.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what lessons from Ukraine have informed the procurement of tactical drones.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The conflict in Ukraine has demonstrated that tactical drones can provide precision and mass at comparatively low cost, but that their effectiveness depends upon the ability to adapt rapidly to battlefield changes, particularly the changes in electronic warfare.

We are applying these lessons by increasing investment in uncrewed and autonomous systems, adopting more agile procurement approaches and strengthening the link between operational users, industry and acquisition. The Strategic Defence Review committed Defence to incorporating uncrewed and autonomous systems into the Integrated Force, while the Defence Investment Plan provides more than £5 billion to accelerate their adoption across the Armed Forces.

This includes investment in inexpensive expendable systems, first-person-view (FPV) and interceptor drones, alongside the establishment of the Uncrewed Systems Centre to help Defence test, procure, field and continually adapt capabilities at greater pace.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what progress his Department has made on delivering the Royal Navy's Hybrid Navy concept.

The Royal Navy's Hybrid Navy will be delivered progressively through a mix of crewed and uncrewed capabilities, supported by £1.5 billion of investment over four years.

Recent progress includes the commissioning of the Royal Navy's first autonomous squadron and the announcement of the Atlantic Net contract, which will integrate commercially delivered autonomous systems and sensors into Royal Navy operations. Future Hybrid Navy capabilities will be introduced progressively, including the first large autonomous vessels by 2030.

writtenQuestions.answerText: The Government does not publish guidance to billing authorities on the use of discretionary powers in the circumstances described. writtenStatements.title: Update on Local Government Best Value
writtenStatements.text:
This Government is committed to shifting power closer to communities, strengthening the role of local and regional government and giving places greater control over the decisions that affect them. This will enable councils and communities to shape better public services, unlock growth, and deliver better outcomes for residents. Strong and accountable local institutions are fundamental to meeting this ambition. That means ensuring councils have the capacity and capability they need to deliver for local people, with this Government taking action to support improvement where necessary.

Today, I am updating the House on the steps we are taking to support eight Councils to recover and reform: Slough, Birmingham, Thurrock, Croydon, Nottingham, Warrington, Newham, and Cheshire East. I have today also published reports on Birmingham, Thurrock, Croydon, Nottingham, and Warrington, alongside my responses.

Slough

On 15 October 2026, the Minister for Local Government, Devolution and Regional Growth announced to the House that the Secretary of State was minded to issue new Directions to Slough Borough Council. These would refresh the Commissioner team, appoint a Political Advisor and establish a ‘one intervention’ approach across MHCLG and DfE, with a single Commissioner team working towards shared objectives across the Authority.

Following consideration of the two representations that were received, and noting the support from the Council for the proposal, the Secretary of State and I have today issued Directions to the Council under section 15(5) and 15(6) of the 1999 Act to implement the proposed intervention package. These come into effect immediately and will remain in force up to and including 30 November 2029. The Directions issued on 20 November 2024 are revoked with immediate effect.

This package, to be in place until 30 November 2029, comprises specific actions the Council is required to undertake. These reflect the priorities identified by the Commissioners' reports and the External Review, which I published on 15 October, including the need to strengthen leadership, governance, secure financial sustainability, build organisational capacity and deliver transformation.

The Secretary of State has nominated four Commissioners appointed to exercise specific Council functions and a Political Advisor: John Coughlan CBE as Lead Commissioner, Debbie Warren as Finance Commissioner, Dr Dave Smith as Managing Director Commissioner, Steve Crocker OBE as Children’s Services Commissioner and William Nunn as Political Advisor.

I would like to put on record my thanks to Gavin Jones CBE, Kim Wright and Denise Murray. I am very grateful to each of them for the expertise, commitment and professionalism they have brought to Slough Borough Council throughout the intervention.

We intend to review the progress of the intervention after 12 months.

Birmingham

Today I am announcing changes to the Birmingham Commissioner team, alongside publishing the Commissioners’ fourth and fifth progress reports, with my response.

The statutory intervention at Birmingham City Council remains necessary due to the significant and ongoing challenges facing the authority, but it is right to recognise the progress achieved over the course of the intervention through the joint working of the Commissioners, council officers, and political leadership. Improvements have been made in advancing the implementation of a new IT system, resolving historic equal pay liabilities, and stabilising Council finances, in part thanks to the work of this Government delivering fairer funding across local government. Notable progress has also been demonstrated in adults' and children's services, evidenced by the Department for Education's SEND intervention stepping down a tier and the Council receiving a second consecutive 'Good' rating from the Care Quality Commission.

Despite this progress, significant challenges remain. Embedding strong governance, a central vision for transformation and an improved culture of decision-making will be vital to bring the Council back in line with the Best Value Duty. The ongoing waste dispute continues to divert capacity from this important work. The Council's objective must now be to redouble its efforts with the Lead Commissioner ensuring that sufficient priority is given to reach a sustainable resolution to the dispute at pace that enables residents to receive a full waste service, is fair to the whole workforce and gives the Council a secure basis for moving forward.

It is also imperative that the Council engages meaningfully with the investigation that launched yesterday into poor-quality supported exempt accommodation in Birmingham, led by Sir David Pearson. Commissioners should provide appropriate oversight and challenge to ensure that the Council engages fully with the investigation, particularly as it relates to the Best Value Duty.

Reflecting the sustained improvement in some areas and the acute challenges that remain in others, I am reconfiguring the intervention team to provide greater focus where it is most needed.

As part of these changes and informed by where significant progress has been made, John Coughlan CBE, Pam Parkes FCIPD, Jackie Belton, Myron Hrycyk and John Biggs will conclude their roles on 30 November 2026. I want to take this opportunity to thank each of them for their professionalism, dedication and important contribution to Birmingham City Council’s improvement journey since the start of the intervention.

As the next phase of the intervention will require a rigorous focus on transformation to ensure the Council's long-term sustainability, I have appointed Kath O'Dwyer as Commissioner to help drive this critical work forward.

It will be important now for the Council to increase the pace of improvement, and we look forward to the Commissioners’ next report in spring next year.

I am also publishing reports from Commissioners and Envoys, alongside the Government's response, in the following areas, and our responses:

Thurrock

The Thurrock Commissioners’ seventh report, published today, describes a ‘substantially stronger organisation’ since Government first intervened in 2022, recognising the sustained commitment to improvement across successive administrations. I welcome the continued improvement through the transition to a new administration and progress in reducing overall debt. Some challenges remain, including securing sustainable financial recovery.

We have recently reduced the level of intervention, with the removal of the Managing Director Commissioner position when the Council appointed a new Chief Executive. We are not at this stage appointing a third Commissioner, as previously proposed, but we will keep this under review. I now look to the Council to build on the progress already underway, take greater ownership of its improvement, address remaining weaknesses and embed sustainable change. I support the Commissioners’ proposed development of an assurance plan, which we look forward to hearing about in their next report in early 2027.

Croydon

We are publishing today the Council and Commissioners’ second progress reports to us since Commissioners were appointed in summer 2025. I would like to thank Mayor Perry, the members and officers at the Council for their continued constructive approach to working with the Commissioner team and developing their improvement plan. The Commissioners’ report outlines a financial position of the London Borough of Croydon which remains extremely challenging. Whilst the Council recognises that their reliance on Exceptional Financial Support to balance their revenue budget is unsustainable, I am concerned that the Council has not yet demonstrated consistent delivery in reducing costs at the necessary scale and pace. Urgent action is now needed to translate plans into delivery. Stronger corporate grip on service improvement and cost reduction will be essential to securing the Council’s long-term financial sustainability.

Nottingham

The Nottingham Envoys’ first report describes encouraging progress including strengthened corporate governance and risk management, with clear evidence that the organisation is putting in place the foundations to drive forward improved outcomes for residents in key service areas. Embedding continuous improvement across the Council is essential, and it is vital that this positive progress is not derailed by poor behaviours which have been highlighted by Envoys. I am confident that, with the continued oversight of Ministerial Envoys and other sector-led support, Nottingham will take the appropriate steps to address these concerns to build and maintain the positive momentum of improvement.

Warrington

I recognise the work of members and officers at Warrington Borough Council to address the significant challenges facing the authority and develop a ‘clear plan for financial recovery’. As the Ministerial Envoys highlight in their second report, the real test is now delivery. The Council must move at pace to deliver savings and transformation, progress the disposal of major commercial assets and implement its refreshed Improvement and Recovery Plan, while continuing to deliver essential services for residents.

We look forward to the Envoys’ next report and expect clear evidence of progress. We will continue to review the intervention arrangements to ensure they remain appropriate.

Best Value Notices

Finally, I am updating the House on two councils that were issued non-statutory Best Value Notices in May 2025, which were subsequently reissued in July 2026.

Cheshire East

The Council has shown signs of improvement, particularly in recent months, with greater focus and momentum behind its improvement work. Progress has also been made in strengthening senior leadership, with a number of permanent appointments made and recruitment underway for a permanent Chief Executive. However, substantial work remains to translate plans into delivery, achieve financial sustainability and embed lasting improvements in governance and culture. I have reissued the Best Value Notice, which will be reviewed again in 12 months, and the Department will continue to monitor the Council’s progress closely.

London Borough of Newham

Following significant progress in strengthening financial management, governance, leadership and service delivery, the Best Value Notice will end with immediate effect. The Department will continue to work with the Council and monitor progress to ensure improvements in financial sustainability, service delivery, governance and organisational culture are sustained and embedded.

Conclusion

We remain committed to supporting all eight councils to secure the sustained improvement needed and deliver better outcomes for local residents.

I will deposit in the House library a copy of the documents referred to, which are being published on gov.uk today. I will update the House in due course.
